original.title: First successful calibration
original.stem_html: A calibration attempt succeeds with probability \(\frac{3}{10}\). Attempts are independent. The random variable \(X\) is the number of attempts made, including the first successful attempt.
original.question_html:
A calibration attempt succeeds with probability \(\frac{3}{10}\). Attempts are independent. The random variable \(X\) is the number of attempts made, including the first successful attempt.

(a)[3]

Derive the probability generating function of \(X\).

(b)[2]

Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\).

(c)[3]

Find the least integer \(N\) for which \(\mathrm P(X<N)>0.98\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Write the probability of \(r-1\) failures followed by one success.

(b)

Evaluate the first derivative at 1.

(c)

Fewer than \(N\) means at most \(N-1\) trials.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Successes on different trials are independent and have the same probability. The count includes the successful trial.

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=\frac{3}{10}\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{r-1},\quad r=1,2,3,\ldots\]

Use the sum of a geometric series:

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3}{10}t\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{7}{10}t\right)^j=\frac{3 t}{10 \left(1 - \frac{7 t}{10}\right)}\]

The series converges for \(|t|<\frac{10}{7}\), so evaluation and differentiation at \(t=1\) are valid.

(b)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{X}'(t)=\frac{30}{\left(7 t - 10\right)^{2}}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_{X}'(1)=\frac{10}{3}\]

(c)

\[\mathrm P(X<N)=1-\left(\frac7{10}\right)^{N-1}\]
\[N-1>\frac{\ln(0.02)}{\ln(0.7)}=10.968034\]

Thus \(N=12\). The preceding integer fails:

\[\mathrm P(X<11)=0.971752,\quad\mathrm P(X<12)=0.980227\]

original.title: Failures before a successful transmission
original.stem_html: A transmitter sends independent messages until one is received correctly. Each message succeeds with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Let \(F\) count only the failed messages before the first success.
original.question_html:
A transmitter sends independent messages until one is received correctly. Each message succeeds with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Let \(F\) count only the failed messages before the first success.

(a)[3]

State the possible values of \(F\) and derive its PGF.

(b)[2]

Find \(\mathrm P(F=4)\) and \(\mathrm P(F\ge3)\).

(c)[2]

Find the greatest positive integer \(n\) for which \(\mathrm P(F<n)<0.97\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

A first-attempt success corresponds to \(F=0\).

(b)

Read the coefficient for an exact count; use consecutive failures for the tail.

(c)

There are \(n\) possible failure counts from 0 to \(n-1\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

Successes on different trials are independent and have the same probability. The count excludes the successful trial.

\[\mathrm P(F=r)=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^r,\quad r=0,1,2,\ldots\]

Use the sum of a geometric series:

\[G_{F}(t)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{3}{5}t\right)^r=\frac{2}{5 \left(1 - \frac{3 t}{5}\right)}\]

The series converges for \(|t|<\frac{5}{3}\), so evaluation and differentiation at \(t=1\) are valid.

(b)

\[\mathrm P(F=4)=\left(\frac35\right)^4\frac25=\frac{162}{3125}\]
\[\mathrm P(F\ge3)=\left(\frac35\right)^3=\frac{27}{125}\]

(c)

\[\mathrm P(F<n)=1-(3/5)^n<0.97\iff n<\frac{\ln(0.03)}{\ln(0.6)}\]

The bound is \(6.864491\), giving \(n=6\). At \(n=7\) the probability already exceeds 0.97.

original.title: Scheduled checks on three days each week
original.stem_html: A laboratory runs an independent diagnostic check every Monday, Wednesday and Friday, beginning on a Monday. The probability that a check detects a fault is a constant \(p\). The probability that the first three checks all fail to detect the fault is 0.343. Let \(X\) be the number of checks until the first detection, including that check.
original.question_html:
A laboratory runs an independent diagnostic check every Monday, Wednesday and Friday, beginning on a Monday. The probability that a check detects a fault is a constant \(p\). The probability that the first three checks all fail to detect the fault is 0.343. Let \(X\) be the number of checks until the first detection, including that check.

(a)[3]

Find \(p\) and derive \(G_X(t)\).

(b)[2]

Find the probability that the first detection is on Friday of the second week.

(c)[3]

Find the least integer \(N\) such that \(\mathrm P(X\le N)>0.96\). State the corresponding day and week.
original.hint_html:
(a)

First determine the failure probability.

(b)

Count checks rather than calendar days.

(c)

Map the final trial number to a three-check week.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(p=3/10,\quad G_X(t)=\frac{3 t}{10 \left(1 - \frac{7 t}{10}\right)}\)

(b)

\(\mathrm P(X=6)=\frac{50421}{1000000}\)

(c)

\(N=10\); Monday of week 4.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[(1-p)^3=0.343=(0.7)^3\Rightarrow p=0.3\]

Successes on different trials are independent and have the same probability. The count includes the successful trial.

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=\frac{3}{10}\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{r-1},\quad r=1,2,3,\ldots\]

Use the sum of a geometric series:

\[G_{X}(t)=\frac{3}{10}t\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{7}{10}t\right)^j=\frac{3 t}{10 \left(1 - \frac{7 t}{10}\right)}\]

The series converges for \(|t|<\frac{10}{7}\), so evaluation and differentiation at \(t=1\) are valid.

(b)

The checks in week 1 are numbers 1, 2, 3; Friday in week 2 is check 6.

\[\mathrm P(X=6)=(0.7)^5(0.3)=\frac{50421}{1000000}\]

(c)

\[1-(0.7)^N>0.96\iff N>\frac{\ln0.04}{\ln0.7}\]

The bound is 9.024676. Hence \(N=10\), which is Monday of week 4.

The probability at \(N-1\) is 0.959646; at \(N\) it is 0.971752.

original.title: Reading a waiting-time distribution from its PGF
original.stem_html:
The number \(X\) of independent attempts needed to authenticate a device has PGF

\[G_X(t)=\frac{t}{4-3t}.\]
original.question_html:
The number \(X\) of independent attempts needed to authenticate a device has PGF

\[G_X(t)=\frac{t}{4-3t}.\]
(a)[2]

Expand the PGF as a geometric series and hence find \(\mathrm P(X\le3)\).

(b)[3]

Find the least integer \(N\) such that \(\mathrm P(X<N)>0.99\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

The coefficient of \(t^r\) is the probability of \(X=r\).

(b)

original.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(t)=\frac t4\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{3t}{4}\right)^j\]

(b)

\[1-(3/4)^{N-1}>0.99\iff N-1>\frac{\ln(0.01)}{\ln(3/4)}\]

The right side is 16.007846. Hence \(N=18\). Check: \(\mathrm P(X<17)=0.989977\) and \(\mathrm P(X<18)=0.992483\).

(a)[2]

(b)[2]

(c)[2]

Given that no success occurs in the first four tests, find the probability that more than nine tests are needed in total.

original.title: Recovering a success probability from the variance
original.stem_html: Independent inspections detect a defect with the same probability \(p\), where \(0<p<1\). Let \(X\) be the number of inspections including the first detection. It is known that \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=12\).
original.question_html:
Independent inspections detect a defect with the same probability \(p\), where \(0<p<1\). Let \(X\) be the number of inspections including the first detection. It is known that \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=12\).

(a)[3]

Derive \(G_X(t)=\dfrac{pt}{1-(1-p)t}\).

(b)[4]

Use derivatives of the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) in terms of \(p\), and hence find \(p\).

(c)[2]

Find \(\mathrm P(3\le X\le6)\).

(d)[2]

Find the least integer \(N\) for which \(\mathrm P(X\le N)>0.99\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use a geometric series with ratio \((1-p)t\).

(b)

Remember the extra first-derivative term in the variance.

(c)

Write the interval event as a difference of two tails.

(d)

Here the successful inspection is allowed to be number \(N\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

For \(r\ge1\), \(\mathrm P(X=r)=p(1-p)^{r-1}\). Therefore

\[G_X(t)=pt\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}[(1-p)t]^j=\frac{pt}{1-(1-p)t}\]

(b)

\[G'_X(1)=\frac1p,\qquad G''_X(1)=\frac{2(1-p)}{p^2}\]
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{2(1-p)}{p^2}+\frac1p-\frac1{p^2}=\frac{1-p}{p^2}\]
\[12p^2+p-1=(4p-1)(3p+1)=0\]

The roots are \(p=1/4\) and \(p=-1/3\). Only \(p=1/4\) is a probability.

(c)

\[\mathrm P(3\le X\le6)=\mathrm P(X>2)-\mathrm P(X>6)=(3/4)^2-(3/4)^6=\frac{1575}{4096}\]

(d)

\[N>\frac{\ln0.01}{\ln(3/4)}\]

Thus \(N=17\). The values at \(N-1\) and \(N\) are 0.989977 and 0.992483 respectively.

(a)[3]

Find \(G_X(t)\) as a polynomial.

(b)[4]

Find \(G_Z(t)\) as an expanded polynomial.

original.question_html:
Independent random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) have PGFs

\[G_X(t)=k(2+t+3t^2),\qquad G_Y(t)=\frac{t(3+2t^2)}5.\]

Let \(Z=X+Y\).

(a)[2]

Find \(k\) and \(\mathrm E(X)\).

(b)[3]

Find \(G_Z(t)\) as an expanded polynomial.

(c)[3]

Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

(d)[1]

State every most probable value of \(Z\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Normalise before differentiating.

(b)

Use the product rule only after identifying the independent variables.

(c)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2\).

(d)

Compare coefficients, not powers.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(k=\frac16,\quad\mathrm E(X)=\frac76\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{t^{5}}{5} + \frac{t^{4}}{15} + \frac{13 t^{3}}{30} + \frac{t^{2}}{10} + \frac{t}{5}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{89}{30},\quad\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{1589}{900}\).

(d)

\(Z=3\) is the unique mode.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(1)=6k=1\Rightarrow k=\frac16\]
\[G'_X(t)=\frac{1+6t}{6},\quad G'_X(1)=\frac76\]

(b)

Independence allows the PGFs to be multiplied:

\[G_{Z}(t)=G_{X}(t)G_{Y}(t)\]
\[=(\frac{t^{2}}{2} + \frac{t}{6} + \frac{1}{3})(\frac{t \left(2 t^{2} + 3\right)}{5})\]
\[=\frac{t^{5}}{5} + \frac{t^{4}}{15} + \frac{13 t^{3}}{30} + \frac{t^{2}}{10} + \frac{t}{5}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{30 t^{4} + 8 t^{3} + 39 t^{2} + 6 t + 6}{30}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{89}{30}\]
\[G_{Z}''(t)=\frac{20 t^{3} + 4 t^{2} + 13 t + 1}{5}\]
\[G_{Z}''(1)=\frac{38}{5}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Z^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2=\frac{1589}{900}\]

(d)

The largest coefficient is \(\frac{13}{30}\), occurring at \(t^{3}\). Therefore \(Z=3\) is the unique mode.

original.title: Combining unequal indicator groups
original.stem_html: A monitoring unit has two identical independent channels, each reporting an event with probability \(1/3\). Their count is \(X\). A second unit has three channels with probabilities \(2/5,\ 2/5,\ 4/5\); their count is \(Y\). All channels are mutually independent. Let \(Z=X+Y\).
original.question_html:
A monitoring unit has two identical independent channels, each reporting an event with probability \(1/3\). Their count is \(X\). A second unit has three channels with probabilities \(2/5,\ 2/5,\ 4/5\); their count is \(Y\). All channels are mutually independent. Let \(Z=X+Y\).

(a)[2]

Find \(G_X(t)\).

(b)[2]

Find \(G_Y(t)\).

(c)[3]

Find \(G_Z(t)\) as an expanded polynomial.

(d)[2]

(e)[1]

(b)

(c)

(d)

Evaluate the first derivative at 1.

(e)

Compare coefficients, not powers.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{9} + \frac{4 t}{9} + \frac{4}{9}\)

(b)

\(G_Y(t)=\frac{16 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{52 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{48 t}{125} + \frac{9}{125}\)

(c)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{16 t^{5}}{1125} + \frac{116 t^{4}}{1125} + \frac{64 t^{3}}{225} + \frac{409 t^{2}}{1125} + \frac{76 t}{375} + \frac{4}{125}\)

(d)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{34}{15}\).

(e)

\(Z=2\) is the unique mode.
original.solution_html:
(a)

For a single indicator with success probability \(p\), the PGF is \(1-p+pt\). Multiply these factors because the indicators are independent.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{t}{3} + \frac{2}{3}\right)\left(\frac{t}{3} + \frac{2}{3}\right)\]
\[=\frac{t^{2}}{9} + \frac{4 t}{9} + \frac{4}{9}\]

(b)

For a single indicator with success probability \(p\), the PGF is \(1-p+pt\). Multiply these factors because the indicators are independent.

\[G_{Y}(t)=\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{4 t}{5} + \frac{1}{5}\right)\]
\[=\frac{16 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{52 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{48 t}{125} + \frac{9}{125}\]

(c)

Independence allows the PGFs to be multiplied:

\[G_{Z}(t)=G_{X}(t)G_{Y}(t)\]
\[=(\frac{t^{2}}{9} + \frac{4 t}{9} + \frac{4}{9})(\frac{16 t^{3}}{125} + \frac{52 t^{2}}{125} + \frac{48 t}{125} + \frac{9}{125})\]
\[=\frac{16 t^{5}}{1125} + \frac{116 t^{4}}{1125} + \frac{64 t^{3}}{225} + \frac{409 t^{2}}{1125} + \frac{76 t}{375} + \frac{4}{125}\]

(d)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{2 \left(t + 2\right) \left(2 t + 3\right) \left(20 t^{2} + 46 t + 19\right)}{1125}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{34}{15}\]

(e)

The largest coefficient is \(\frac{409}{1125}\), occurring at \(t^{2}\). Therefore \(Z=2\) is the unique mode.

original.title: Deriving the Poisson generating function
original.stem_html: Let \(X\) have a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda>0\). You may use the series \(e^z=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}z^r/r!\).
original.question_html:
Let \(X\) have a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda>0\). You may use the series \(e^z=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}z^r/r!\).

(a)[3]

Starting from the probability mass function, prove that \(G_X(t)=e^{\lambda(t-1)}\).

(b)[3]

Use this PGF to obtain the mean and variance of \(X\).

(c)[2]

By evaluating \(G_X(-1)\), find the probability that \(X\) is even. Include zero as even.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Recognise the exponential series after factoring out \(e^{-\lambda}\).

(b)

The second derivative at 1 is \(\lambda^2\), not the variance.

(c)

Separate the defining series into even and odd powers.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^r}{r!},\quad r=0,1,2,\ldots\]
\[G_X(t)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^r t^r}{r!}=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda t}=e^{\lambda(t-1)}\]

(b)

\[G'_X(t)=\lambda e^{\lambda(t-1)},\quad G''_X(t)=\lambda^2 e^{\lambda(t-1)}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=\lambda,\quad\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda^2+\lambda-\lambda^2=\lambda\]

(c)

Since \((-1)^r\) is +1 for even \(r\) and −1 for odd \(r\),

\[G_X(-1)=P_{\rm even}-P_{\rm odd}=e^{-2\lambda},\qquad P_{\rm even}+P_{\rm odd}=1\]
\[P_{\rm even}=\frac{1+e^{-2\lambda}}2\]

original.title: One-point activations and two-point die outcomes
original.stem_html: Three independent indicators have success probabilities \(1/4,\ 1/2,\ 2/3\). Let \(X\) count successes. A fair eight-sided die labelled 1 to 8 is rolled independently twice, and \(Y\) counts rolls showing either 6 or 8. The two experiments are independent. A score is defined by \(Z=X+2Y\).
original.question_html:
Three independent indicators have success probabilities \(1/4,\ 1/2,\ 2/3\). Let \(X\) count successes. A fair eight-sided die labelled 1 to 8 is rolled independently twice, and \(Y\) counts rolls showing either 6 or 8. The two experiments are independent. A score is defined by \(Z=X+2Y\).

(a)[3]

Find \(G_X(t)\).

(b)[4]

Using the definition of a PGF for \(2Y\), find \(G_Z(t)\) as a polynomial.

(c)[2]

Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use one Bernoulli factor for each indicator.

(b)

Each counted die outcome contributes two points.

(c)

Evaluate the first derivative at 1.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{t^{3}}{12} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{8} + \frac{5 t}{12} + \frac{1}{8}\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{t^{7}}{192} + \frac{3 t^{6}}{128} + \frac{11 t^{5}}{192} + \frac{19 t^{4}}{128} + \frac{13 t^{3}}{64} + \frac{33 t^{2}}{128} + \frac{15 t}{64} + \frac{9}{128}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{29}{12}\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

For a single indicator with success probability \(p\), the PGF is \(1-p+pt\). Multiply these factors because the indicators are independent.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{t}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\right)\left(\frac{t}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{2 t}{3} + \frac{1}{3}\right)\]
\[=\frac{t^{3}}{12} + \frac{3 t^{2}}{8} + \frac{5 t}{12} + \frac{1}{8}\]

(b)

A successful die roll has probability \(2/8=1/4\).

\[G_Y(t)=\left(\frac{t}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}\]
\[G_{2Y}(t)=\mathrm E[(t^2)^Y]=G_Y(t^2)\]
\[G_Z(t)=G_X(t)G_Y(t^2)=\frac{t^{7}}{192} + \frac{3 t^{6}}{128} + \frac{11 t^{5}}{192} + \frac{19 t^{4}}{128} + \frac{13 t^{3}}{64} + \frac{33 t^{2}}{128} + \frac{15 t}{64} + \frac{9}{128}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{\left(t^{2} + 3\right) \left(7 t^{4} + 27 t^{3} + 34 t^{2} + 33 t + 15\right)}{192}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{29}{12}\]

original.stem_html:
Independent variables \(X\) and \(Y\) have PGFs

\[G_X(t)=\frac{t}{(2-t)^3},\qquad G_Y(t)=\frac{t^2}{(2-t)^2}.\]

Let \(Z=X+Y\).
original.question_html:
Independent variables \(X\) and \(Y\) have PGFs

\[G_X(t)=\frac{t}{(2-t)^3},\qquad G_Y(t)=\frac{t^2}{(2-t)^2}.\]

Let \(Z=X+Y\).

(a)[5]

(b)[5]

(a)

(b)

(a)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{X}'(t)=\frac{2 \left(t + 1\right)}{\left(t - 2\right)^{4}}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_{X}'(1)=4\]
\[G_{X}''(t)=- \frac{6 \left(t + 2\right)}{\left(t - 2\right)^{5}}\]
\[G_{X}''(1)=18\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2=6\]

Find \(G_X(t)\).

original.title: Reconstructing a missing coefficient in a PGF
original.stem_html:
The variable \(Y\) is the sum of two independent observations of a non-negative integer-valued variable \(X\). Its PGF is

\[G_Y(t)=\frac{4+20t+25t^2+4t^3+10t^4+t^6}{64}.\]
original.question_html:
The variable \(Y\) is the sum of two independent observations of a non-negative integer-valued variable \(X\). Its PGF is

\[G_Y(t)=\frac{4+20t+25t^2+4t^3+10t^4+t^6}{64}.\]
(a)[3]

Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

(b)[4]

Find \(G_X(t)\) as a polynomial. Explain why the sign of its constant coefficient is fixed.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2\).

(b)

Use coefficients in increasing order and non-negativity.
original.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Y}'(t)=\frac{\left(3 t^{2} + 5\right) \left(t^{3} + 5 t + 2\right)}{32}\]
\[\mathrm E(Y)=G_{Y}'(1)=2\]
\[G_{Y}''(t)=\frac{15 t^{4} + 60 t^{2} + 12 t + 25}{32}\]
\[G_{Y}''(1)=\frac{7}{2}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Y^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=G_{Y}''(1)+G_{Y}'(1)-[G_{Y}'(1)]^2=\frac{3}{2}\]

(b)

The highest possible value of \(Y\) is 6, so the highest possible value of each identically distributed non-negative summand is 3. Write \(G_X(t)=a+bt+ct^2+dt^3\). Its coefficients are probabilities and cannot be negative.

\[a^2=\frac4{64}\Rightarrow a=\frac14\]
\[2ab=\frac{20}{64}\Rightarrow b=\frac58\]
\[b^2+2ac=\frac{25}{64}\Rightarrow c=0\]
\[2ad+2bc=\frac4{64}\Rightarrow d=\frac18\]
\[G_X(t)=\frac{t^{3}}{8} + \frac{5 t}{8} + \frac{1}{4}\]

Squaring this polynomial reproduces every coefficient of \(G_Y\).

Find \(a\) and \(b\).

(b)[3]

original.title: Two repeated binary experiments
original.stem_html: A binary experiment A succeeds with probability \(2/5\) and is performed twice. Let \(X\) count successes. Independently, binary experiment B succeeds with probability \(1/2\) and is performed twice; \(Y\) counts its successes. All four trials are independent, and \(Z=X+Y\).
original.question_html:
A binary experiment A succeeds with probability \(2/5\) and is performed twice. Let \(X\) count successes. Independently, binary experiment B succeeds with probability \(1/2\) and is performed twice; \(Y\) counts its successes. All four trials are independent, and \(Z=X+Y\).

(a)[2]

Find \(G_X(t)\).

(b)[3]

Find \(G_Z(t)\) as an expanded polynomial.

(c)[3]

Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(Z)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\).

(d)[1]

State every most probable value of \(Z\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use two identical independent factors.

(b)

Use the product rule only after identifying the independent variables.

(c)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2\).

(d)

Compare coefficients, not powers.
original.answer_html:
(a)

\(G_X(t)=\frac{4 t^{2}}{25} + \frac{12 t}{25} + \frac{9}{25}\)

(b)

\(G_Z(t)=\frac{t^{4}}{25} + \frac{t^{3}}{5} + \frac{37 t^{2}}{100} + \frac{3 t}{10} + \frac{9}{100}\)

(c)

\(\mathrm E(Z)=\frac{9}{5},\quad\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{49}{50}\).

(d)

\(Z=2\) is the unique mode.
original.solution_html:
(a)

For a single indicator with success probability \(p\), the PGF is \(1-p+pt\). Multiply these factors because the indicators are independent.

\[G_{X}(t)=\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{2 t}{5} + \frac{3}{5}\right)\]
\[=\frac{4 t^{2}}{25} + \frac{12 t}{25} + \frac{9}{25}\]

(b)

Independence allows the PGFs to be multiplied:

\[G_{Z}(t)=G_{X}(t)G_{Y}(t)\]
\[=(\frac{4 t^{2}}{25} + \frac{12 t}{25} + \frac{9}{25})(\frac{t^{2}}{4} + \frac{t}{2} + \frac{1}{4})\]
\[=\frac{t^{4}}{25} + \frac{t^{3}}{5} + \frac{37 t^{2}}{100} + \frac{3 t}{10} + \frac{9}{100}\]

(c)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{Z}'(t)=\frac{\left(t + 1\right) \left(2 t + 3\right) \left(4 t + 5\right)}{50}\]
\[\mathrm E(Z)=G_{Z}'(1)=\frac{9}{5}\]
\[G_{Z}''(t)=\frac{24 t^{2} + 60 t + 37}{50}\]
\[G_{Z}''(1)=\frac{121}{50}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(Z^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(Z)=G_{Z}''(1)+G_{Z}'(1)-[G_{Z}'(1)]^2=\frac{49}{50}\]

(d)

The largest coefficient is \(\frac{37}{100}\), occurring at \(t^{2}\). Therefore \(Z=2\) is the unique mode.

original.stem_html: A variable \(X\) takes values 0, 1 and 3 with probabilities \(a\), \(3a\) and \(b\) respectively, where \(a,b\ge0\) and \(4a+b=1\). Let \(Y=X_1+\cdots+X_8\), where the \(X_i\) are independent observations of \(X\).
original.question_html:
A variable \(X\) takes values 0, 1 and 3 with probabilities \(a\), \(3a\) and \(b\) respectively, where \(a,b\ge0\) and \(4a+b=1\). Let \(Y=X_1+\cdots+X_8\), where the \(X_i\) are independent observations of \(X\).

(a)[2]

Write down \(G_X(t)\) and use it to find \(\mathrm E(X)\).

(b)[3]

Show that \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=6b+3(a+b)-9(a+b)^2\).

(c)[3]

Use the PGF of \(Y\) to prove that \(\mathrm E(Y)=8\mathrm E(X)\).

(d)[2]

When \(b=0\), identify the distribution of \(Y\) fully.
original.hint_html:
(a)

The power is 3 for the last supported value.

(b)

Use the second factorial moment, not the raw second moment.

(c)

Use the product/chain rule and the normalisation constraint.

(d)

Find \(a\) first in the boundary case.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(t)=a+3at+bt^3,\qquad G_X^{\prime}(t)=3a+3bt^2\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_X^{\prime}(1)=3a+3b\]

(b)

\[G_X^{\prime\prime}(t)=6bt,\quad G_X^{\prime\prime}(1)=6b\]
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=6b+(3a+3b)-(3a+3b)^2\]

(c)

\[G_Y(t)=[G_X(t)]^8,\qquad G_Y^{\prime}(t)=8[G_X(t)]^7G_X^{\prime}(t)\]

Since \(G_X(1)=4a+b=1\),

original.question_html:
A variable \(X\) takes values 1 and 3 with probabilities \(3/5\) and \(2/5\). The variable \(Y\) is the sum of five independent observations of \(X\).

(a)[1]

(b)[2]

Give \(G_Y(t)\) in factorised form and state its support.

(c)[3]

(d)[4]

(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

original.question_html:
The variable \(X\) is discrete uniform on \(\{0,1,2,3,4\}\). Let \(X_1,X_2,X_3\) be independent observations of \(X\), and set \(S=X_1+X_2+X_3\).

(a)[3]

Find \(G_X(t)\) both as a polynomial and as a single fraction for \(t\ne1\). State its value at \(t=1\).

(b)[3]

Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

(c)[3]

Use the PGF of \(S\) to find \(\mathrm P(S=4)\).

(d)[3]

Given that \(S=4\), find \(\mathrm P(X_1=0\mid S=4)\).
original.hint_html:
(a)

Use the finite geometric-sum identity, without treating \(t=1\) as undefined for the PGF.

(b)

Use \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2\).

(c)

Only the coefficient of degree 4 is needed; do not expand unnecessary higher powers.

(d)

Use the joint probability in the numerator, not the marginal \(\mathrm P(X_1=0)\).
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_X(t)=\frac15(1+t+t^2+t^3+t^4)\]

Sum the finite geometric progression:

\[G_X(t)=\frac{1-t^5}{5(1-t)},\quad t\ne1\]

The fraction has a removable singularity at 1. The defining polynomial gives \(G_X(1)=1\).

(b)

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{X}'(t)=\frac{4 t^{3} + 3 t^{2} + 2 t + 1}{5}\]
\[\mathrm E(X)=G_{X}'(1)=2\]
\[G_{X}''(t)=\frac{2 \left(6 t^{2} + 3 t + 1\right)}{5}\]
\[G_{X}''(1)=4\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=G_{X}''(1)+G_{X}'(1)-[G_{X}'(1)]^2=2\]

(c)

\[G_S(t)=\frac{(1+t+t^2+t^3+t^4)^3}{125}\]

To obtain degree 4, the three exponents must be non-negative and sum to 4; none can then exceed 4. There are \(\binom{6}{2}=15\) such ordered triples. Equivalently, direct multiplication gives coefficient 15.

\[\mathrm P(S=4)=\frac{15}{125}=\frac3{25}\]

(d)

With \(X_1=0\), the other two values must sum to 4. The five ordered pairs are \((0,4),(1,3),(2,2),(3,1),(4,0)\).

\[\mathrm P(X_1=0,S=4)=\frac15\cdot\frac5{25}=\frac1{25}\]
\[\mathrm P(X_1=0\mid S=4)=\frac{1/25}{3/25}=\frac13\]

original.question_html:
A variable \(X\) takes values 0, 1 and 3 only. Its mean is \(5/4\) and its variance is \(19/16\). Let \(Y\) be the sum of three independent observations of \(X\).

(a)[4]

Find all three probabilities and hence \(G_X(t)\).

(b)[2]

Find \(G_Y(t)\) in factorised form and \(\mathrm E(Y)\).

(c)[2]

Find \(\mathrm P(Y=3)\).

(b)

original.question_html:
A variable \(Y\) is the sum of two independent observations of a non-negative integer-valued variable \(X\). Its PGF is

\[G_Y(t)=\frac{t^2}{(5-4t)^2}.\]

(b)[2]

Use the PGF to find \(\mathrm E(X)\).

(c)[2]

Find \(\mathrm P(X>5)\).

(a)

A PGF must have non-negative coefficients and value 1 at t=1.

(b)

Evaluate the first derivative at 1.

(c)

Read the geometric failure probability from the power series.

(a)

\[[G_X(t)]^2=G_Y(t)\Rightarrow G_X(t)=\frac{t}{5-4t}\]

\[G_X(t)=\frac t5\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac45t\right)^j\]

This is a waiting-time distribution with success probability \(1/5\). More than 5 trials requires five failures, so

\[\mathrm P(X>5)=(4/5)^5=1024/3125\]

(a)

\(G_A(t)=\frac{2 t^{6}}{5} + \frac{2 t^{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{5}\)

(b)

(c)

(b)

Every value of \(A\) is even. For \(B=3\), the possible ordered pairs are (0,3) and (3,0). Hence

\[\mathrm P(A=3)=0,\quad\mathrm P(B=3)=2\cdot\frac15\cdot\frac25=\frac4{25}\]

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(A^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(A)=G_{A}''(1)+G_{A}'(1)-[G_{A}'(1)]^2=\frac{144}{25}\]

Differentiate the PGF, then evaluate at \(t=1\).

\[G_{B}'(t)=\frac{4 \left(3 t^{2} + 1\right) \left(2 t^{3} + 2 t + 1\right)}{25}\]

\[G_{B}''(t)=\frac{8 \left(15 t^{4} + 12 t^{2} + 3 t + 1\right)}{25}\]
\[G_{B}''(1)=\frac{248}{25}\]

The second derivative gives the factorial moment, not \(\mathrm E(B^2)\).

\[\operatorname{Var}(B)=G_{B}''(1)+G_{B}'(1)-[G_{B}'(1)]^2=\frac{72}{25}\]

The means are equal, but the variance of \(A\) is twice that of \(B\). Reusing the same observation creates perfect dependence.

original.title: A central coefficient and a conditional event
original.stem_html: The variables \(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4\) are independent and each is discrete uniform on \(\{0,1,2\}\). Let \(S=X_1+X_2+X_3+X_4\).
original.question_html:
The variables \(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4\) are independent and each is discrete uniform on \(\{0,1,2\}\). Let \(S=X_1+X_2+X_3+X_4\).

(a)[3]

Use the PGF of \(S\) to find \(\mathrm P(S=4)\).

(b)[2]

Given that \(S=4\), find the probability that all four observations are equal.

(c)[2]

A student claims that \(S\) has the same distribution as \(4X_1\) because their means are equal. Refute the claim using PGFs.
original.hint_html:
(a)

Square the quadratic once, then extract one coefficient from the second square.

(b)

The condition on the total removes the all-zero and all-two cases.

(c)

The same observation used four times is not four independent observations.
original.solution_html:
(a)

\[G_S(t)=\frac{(1+t+t^2)^4}{81}\]

First square once: \((1+t+t^2)^2=1+2t+3t^2+2t^3+t^4\). The degree-4 coefficient in its square is

\[1\cdot1+2\cdot2+3\cdot3+2\cdot2+1\cdot1=19\]
\[\mathrm P(S=4)=\frac{19}{81}\]

(b)

Four equal observations with total 4 must all equal 1. This particular outcome has probability \((1/3)^4=1/81\). Therefore

\[\mathrm P(X_1=X_2=X_3=X_4\mid S=4)=\frac{1/81}{19/81}=\frac1{19}\]

(c)

\[G_{4X_1}(t)=\mathrm E[(t^4)^{X_1}]=G_{X_1}(t^4)=\frac{1+t^4+t^8}{3}\]

Its probability of a total 4 is \(1/3\), whereas \(\mathrm P(S=4)=19/81\). Equal means do not determine an entire distribution.
